title: SLM Architecture
intro:
Small Language Models (SLMs) generally use a Transformer-based architecture, similar to larger LLMs, but with fewer parameters and a more efficient design. The core components include tokenization, embeddings, Transformer layers, attention mechanisms, and an output layer that generates predictions.

SLMs may use fewer Transformer layers, smaller hidden dimensions, fewer attention heads, or optimized attention mechanisms to reduce computational and memory requirements. Techniques such as quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) can further improve efficiency.

sections.heading: The End-to-End Pipeline
sections.body:
At a high level, almost every Transformer-based language model — whether it is a Small Language Model (SLM) or a Large Language Model (LLM) — follows the same fundamental pipeline: text is converted into numbers, processed through a series of Transformer blocks, and converted back into probabilities for predicting the next token.

The main components are:

  • Tokenizer — converts raw text into smaller units called tokens. These may be words, subwords, or even individual characters, depending on the tokenizer. Techniques such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) and SentencePiece allow the model to represent a large and flexible vocabulary without needing a separate entry for every possible word.
  • Embedding Layer — converts each token into a dense numerical vector called an embedding. Positional information is also incorporated so the model can understand both what each token represents and where it appears in the sequence.
  • Transformer Blocks × N — these repeated blocks form the computational core of the model. Through mechanisms such as self-attention and feed-forward neural networks, each block allows the model to build increasingly rich representations of the context. SLMs generally achieve their smaller footprint by using fewer layers, smaller hidden dimensions, and/or fewer attention heads compared with larger models.
  • Final LayerNorm + Output Head — after passing through all Transformer blocks, the final hidden representation is normalized and projected into the model's vocabulary space. A softmax function then converts these scores (logits) into probabilities for the possible next tokens, allowing the model to select or sample its next prediction.

In simple terms, the journey looks like this:

Text → Tokens → Embeddings → Transformer Blocks → Next-Token Probabilities

sections.heading: Inside a Transformer Block
sections.body:
Each Transformer block repeats the same internal pattern twice: normalize, transform, and add the result back onto the original input. This "residual connection" is what lets models — including quite shallow SLMs — train stably with a reasonably direct path for gradients to flow back through the network.

  • Multi-head self-attention — lets every token look at every other token in the sequence and decide how much attention to pay to each one, which is how the model builds context and handles things like pronoun references or long-range dependencies.
  • Feed-forward network — a small two-layer MLP applied independently to each token position, typically using a GeLU or SwiGLU activation, giving the model extra capacity to transform what attention has gathered.
  • LayerNorm + residual add — wraps both sub-layers, stabilizing training and preserving information from earlier in the network.

SLMs often make this block cheaper without changing its basic shape — shrinking the hidden dimension, reducing the number of attention heads, or sharing key/value projections across heads (grouped-query or multi-query attention) so there's less to store and compute at inference time.

sections.heading: Design Choices That Keep SLMs Small
sections.body:
Beyond simply using fewer and narrower layers, most practical SLMs lean on a handful of techniques to pack as much capability as possible into a small parameter budget:

  • Knowledge distillation — training the small model to mimic the output distribution of a much larger "teacher" model, often recovering far more capability than training on raw text alone would allow at that size.
  • Quantization — storing and computing weights at lower numerical precision (INT8, INT4, or similar), cutting memory and bandwidth needs with a relatively small accuracy trade-off.
  • Pruning — removing weights, attention heads, or entire layers that contribute little to the output, either before or after training.
  • Parameter sharing — reusing the same weights across multiple layers or attention heads instead of learning separate ones, trading a small amount of expressiveness for a meaningfully smaller model.
